list.listitem: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is most common in children younger than 5 years and occurs rarely in adults. B
SSSS is caused by a circulating exfoliative exotoxin, produced by some strains of Staphyloccus aureus. B
SSSS often begins with a prodrome of fever and irritability. A tender erythematous rash then develops. Bullae and superficial desquamation soon follow. C
Antibiotics effective against known resistant strains of Staphylococcus aureus should be promptly started. B
Supportive care, including attention to skin care, temperature control, pain management, fluid loss, and nutrition is important. B
Overall mortality is low in children with appropriate treatment. Occurence in adults in associated with underlying comorbidity and higher mortality. B

background.definition: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is a clinical term used to describe a spectrum of blistering skin diseases caused by the exfoliative toxins of Staphylococcus aureus. It is most commonly seen in infants and children and rarely in adults. The exfoliative toxin involved in SSSS leads to cleavage of desmoglein 1, a desmosomal protein involved in intercellular adhesion. This leads to blistering of the upper layer of skin. The same toxins are responsible for bullous impetigo.

list.listitem: The annual incidence is around 7.5 per 100,000 in infants less than 1 year old. The annual incidence is much lower in adults.
Endemic outbreaks of SSSS have occurred in hospital nurseries.
SSSS is comparatively rare in adults and is associated with underlying comorbidity. Classic associations in adults include kidney disease and immunosuppression.
SSSS is caused by the release of exfoliative exotoxins from some strains of S. aureus.

The source of primary infection may not be evident. SSSS may also be caused by a clinically evident infection, such as an abscess or wound site, or may be caused by colonization of toxin-producing S. aureus in the axilla, nose, perineum, and toe webs.
S. aureus is common in the general population (including in children), with many people being commensal carriers.
Some strains of S. aureus produce toxins, known as exfoliative exotoxins, which can act on the skin and lead to the formation of vesicles and blisters.
When the exfoliative exotoxins act locally, the clinical presentation is bullous impetigo. Circulating toxin effect leads to the more generalized clinical presentation of SSSS.
Two exfoliative exotoxins have been identified, exfoliative exotoxin A (ETA) and exfoliative exotoxin B (ETB). In the Western Hemisphere, the majority of toxin-producing isolates produce ETA.
The exfoliative toxins target desmoglein 1 (a cadherin important in keratinocytic adhesion), leading to epidermolysis (acantholysis) histologically and vesicle and blister formation clinically.
The toxins produce intraepidermal cleavage (acantholysis/epidermolysis with separation) at the level of the stratum granulosum.
SSSS occurs most commonly in children younger than 5 years and is much less common in adults. B

SSSS is primarily a clinical diagnosis with fever and irritability followed by a tender erythematous rash with peeling of the outer layer of skin at the stratum granulosum. Histological examination is confirmatory. B
A classic physical exam finding is radial perioral erythema, crusting, and fissuring. B

SSSS needs to be differentiated from other items on the differential, especially toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or other drug eruptions. TEN is more common in adults, generally associated with drug/medication use, has more extensive mucosal involvement, and has different histological features on microscopy. Skin biopsy can be used to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other conditions. In contrast to toxic epidermolytic necrolysis (TEN), necrosis is minimal to absent and the level of separation is more superficial. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Often extensive mucosal involvement, full-thickness dermal necrosis including along the basal layer histologically, associated with drug ingestion
History and location, histology shows variable epidermal and dermal change
Papular, "sandpaper" rash, any peeling is late in the course
Various types all have deeper planes of separation with different clinical appearance and histology
Clinical history of drug exposure, less desquamation, different biopsy findings
Very rare in children, can be separated by light microscopy and immunofluorescence studies if there is clinical concern
Lacks extensive blister formation, lacks perioral crusting, associated with multisystem involvement
Associated with conjunctival injection, oral mucosa erythema, strawberry tongue, lymphadenopathy, rash without extensive blister formation

list.listitem: There is often a short prodrome of malaise, irritability, poor intake, conjunctivitus, sometimes with fever or upper respiratory symptoms.
Cutaneous findings are initially of erythema, sometimes widespread but especially around folds (neck, axilla, intertriginous skin), with skin pain/tenderness.
Erythema eventuates into fine "tissue paper-like" superficial vesicles which then form blisters with peeling.
A classic physical exam finding is radial perioral fissuring, scale, and crusting.
A common finding is the Nikolsky sign. This sign is positive when gentle lateral pressure on the skin causes superficial separation.

The areas of bullae and erosion generally spread over a couple of days. The conjunctiva can sometimes be involved, but usually mucous membranes are largely spared. This is in contrast to the typical presentation of SJS.
With treatment, the process resolves within several days (less than 2 weeks). Because the insult is superficial, healing is comparatively fast and non-scarring.
In the classic setting with characteristic findings and without suspicion for an alternative diagnosis, the diagnosis may be entirely clinical (based on history and physical exam).

In uncertain or equivocal cases, skin biopsy is helpful in ruling out other conditions and confirming the diagnosis. Immunofluorescence studies may be considered if there is clinical concern for autoimmune blistering disease.
Aerobic bacterial cultures of sites suspicious for primary infection can be supportive of the diagnosis if positive and can also help guide therapy.
Blood cultures are rarely positive in children but may be more commonly positive for S. aureus in adults.
SSSS is generally a clinical diagnosis with fever, irritability followed by a tender erythematous rash, and then superficial peeling and blister formation.
Although diagnostic testing is not always necessary, diagnosis can be confirmed or supported by skin biopsy.
Early treatment is with antibiotics that have activity against S. aureus (such as nafcillin, oxacillin, or flucloxacillin).A

In areas of endemic methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), initial antibiotic coverage may be broad (eg, IV clindamycin or vancomycin) and narrowed if sensitivity results are available. B
Good local skin care, temperature control, pain management, fluid management, nutrition, and secondary infection all should be addressed and managed. C
Prompt initiation of antibiotics with activity against S. aureus (such as nafcillin, oxacillin, flucloxacillin) in the hospital.
The emergence of MRSA in some areas should be considered, especially in a patient who is not improving.

Antibacterial coverage should be directed against S. aureus using penicillinase resistant antibiotics such as nafcillin or oxacillin. In areas of high resistance, consideration may be given to MRSA coverage. In most areas of the United States, this would be with clindamycin. If clindamycin resistance is present in the community or if the patient is unstable, IV vancomycin should be considered. Antibiotic coverage can be adjusted after culture sensitivity results return.
If the patient worsens, consider blood cultures to look for bacteremia and broadening antibiotic spectrum.

Patients should be admitted to the hospital for antibiotics and wound care. Topical care includes bland emollients and nonadherent bandages changed daily. Order contact isolation, minimal handling of the patient, and avoidance of tape in affected areas.
Supportive care: fluid and electrolytes should be closely monitored because of increased fluid loss.
Monitor nutritional care: most patients can get adequate calories orally.
Monitor pain and treat adequately.
All patients should be admitted to the hospital for appropriate antibiotic therapy.
All patients should be monitored closely for excessive fluid losses, pain control, and secondary infections.

Since the level of skin cleavage is superficial, patients can be admitted to a general pediatric floor as long as they can receive adequate contact isolation. For patients with severe cases admission to an intensive care unit or burn unit should be considered.
Consultation with a dermatologist for help with diagnosis and management and/or an infectious disease specialist for help with empiric therapy should be considered.
Infection control should be consulted for infections that occur in nurseries.
Treatment in the hospital should continue until the skin begins to heal, the patient can maintain fluid balance and nutrition orally, and caregivers can be responsible for wound and skin care.
The vast majority of children recover fully from SSSS with no sequelae. The mortality rate for children is low with appropriate treatment. B
The mortality rate from SSSS may be higher in adults. Many cases in adults occur in patients with significant underlying disease and comorbidity, classically renal disease and immunosuppression. C
SSSS is much less common in adults.
Most adults with SSSS have chronic underlying comorbidites.
Mortality rates may be higher in adults.
